historical_timeline.summary: Began studying Western medicine at the Boji Hospital in Guangzhou.
Entered the College of Medicine for Chinese in Hong Kong.
Received his medical diploma at the college's first graduation ceremony.
Moved his medical practice from Macau to Guangzhou.
Founded the China Revival Society in Honolulu; left medicine for politics.
Founded the Chinese Revolutionary League in Tokyo.
Became Provisional President of the Republic of China in Nanjing.
Presided over the First National Congress of the Kuomintang in Guangzhou.
Arrived in Beijing in poor health.
Admitted to the Peking Union Medical College Hospital; exploratory laparotomy found carcinoma involving the liver.
Limited autopsy reported adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder with spread to the liver and beyond.

claims.statement: Sun Yat-sen was born on November 12, 1866, into an ordinary farming family in Cuiheng Village. He was called Dixiang in childhood and also had the names Mingwen, Deming and Rixin; the name Yat-sen came into use while he was in Japan.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The birth date used for the synthetic date of birth.

source_links.locator: Introduction to the Museum of Dr. Sun Yat-sen

claims.statement: He went to a private school at nine, studied in Honolulu from the age of thirteen, and returned home at seventeen.

He began studying Western medicine at the Boji Hospital in Guangzhou in 1886 and in 1887 transferred to the College of Medicine for Chinese in Hong Kong, as one of its twelve students; his teachers included Patrick Manson. He was one of two students who passed the graduation examination in 1892 and received his diploma at the college's first graduation ceremony on July 23, 1892.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern episode's physician-as-patient theme.

source_links.locator: 1886 Boji Hospital; 1887 Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese

claims.statement: After graduating he practiced medicine in Macau, first at the Kiang Wu Hospital and then in a dispensary of his own, and then in Guangzhou, opening pharmacies that offered Chinese and Western medicines; about two years after graduating he gave up medicine for politics.
claims.clinical_interpretation: He practiced for about two years; the modern episode treats him as a physician by training who left practice decades ago.

source_links.locator: settled in Macau; moved to Guangzhou in 1893; closed his practice about a year later
practiced in Macau, Shiqi and Guangzhou

claims.statement: In 1894 he founded the China Revival Society in Honolulu; in 1905 he founded the Chinese Revolutionary League in Tokyo; on New Year's Day 1912 he became Provisional President of the Republic of China in Nanjing; and in January 1924 he presided over the First National Congress of the Kuomintang in Guangzhou.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Social history: the anchor for the modern work as the leader of a political organization.

source_links.locator: January 1924, First National Congress of the Kuomintang

claims.statement: In the autumn of 1924, after the Beijing Coup, he was invited to Beijing to discuss state affairs, and he arrived in Beijing in poor health on the last day of 1924.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the true-frame episode; history only.

source_links.locator: On the last day of 1924, Sun Yat-sen, in poor health, came to Beijing

claims.statement: Several months before his operation in January 1925 a mass had been noted in his right upper abdomen and was thought to be his liver; it grew larger shortly before surgery. At the preoperative examination he had no jaundice and not much loss of weight.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern presenting problem, a right upper quadrant mass. The month the mass was first noted is not recorded.

claims.statement: He was admitted to the Peking Union Medical College Hospital on January 26, 1925, too ill to eat, and had an exploratory laparotomy that day by Adrian S. Taylor, the head of surgery, which found extensive involvement of the liver by carcinoma. He was treated with radium for the rest of his stay, left the hospital against advice on February 18, 1925, and was then treated by old-style Chinese doctors while his condition declined.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; after the true-frame episode.

source_links.locator: hospitalized on January 26th 1925, at which point, he was too ill to eat

claims.statement: He died in Beijing on March 12, 1925.
His fatal illness has long been described as liver cancer, the diagnosis taken from the findings at the laparotomy; the museum at his birthplace states that he died of liver cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as the traditional account; a later review of the autopsy report disputes a primary liver cancer (CLM-0011).

source_links.locator: died of liver cancer in Beijing
mistakenly believed on the basis of the laparotomy observations

claims.statement: A limited autopsy at the Peking Union Medical College Hospital on March 13, 1925, by James R. Cash, reported adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder with obstruction of the cystic duct, direct extension to the liver and diaphragm, and metastases to the lungs, peritoneum, ileum and colon, with healed cholecystitis, gallstones, generalized arteriosclerosis, healed calcified tuberculosis of the lungs, emphysema, ascites and roundworm infestation. A 2016 review concludes that gallbladder adenocarcinoma, not a primary liver cancer, caused his death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern diagnosis: a gallbladder adenocarcinoma that invades the liver and presents as a liver mass. The review rests on the autopsy report; the original slides were not re-examined in the fetched source.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a 57-year-old physician by training, now a political leader, who presents with a right upper quadrant mass and weight loss: the work-up of a solid liver mass (multiphase imaging, alpha-fetoprotein, CA 19-9 and CEA, hepatitis B and C serology, liver function with Child-Pugh and ALBI scoring, and biopsy because a mass in a non-cirrhotic liver cannot be diagnosed by imaging alone, following the AASLD 2023 guidance), the finding of a gallbladder adenocarcinoma invading the liver rather than a primary liver cancer (mirroring the historical conflict between the operative and autopsy findings), staging laparoscopy and the multidisciplinary tumor board on the NCCN biliary tract cancers guideline, first-line gemcitabine, cisplatin and durvalumab with its monitoring, hepatitis B reactivation monitoring in resolved infection, early specialist palliative care, and the care of a physician as a patient.

visit_schedule.purpose: New patient with a right upper abdominal mass, aching and weight loss: work-up of a liver mass, symptom care, and how he wants to receive results
Biopsy and imaging results and medical oncology consultation; diagnosis, staging plan, and hepatitis B status
Staging laparoscopy result and tumor board recommendation; first cycle of chemoimmunotherapy and specialist palliative care
Before cycle 4: restaging CT, tumor marker, toxicity review, hepatitis B monitoring, and genomic profiling result
Same-day sick visit for a cold during chemoimmunotherapy
Before cycle 8: restaging CT, toxicity review, low magnesium, and the plan for maintenance durvalumab

problems.display: Right upper quadrant abdominal mass with weight loss: a dull ache under the right ribs and early fullness for about three months, 4 kg weight loss, and a firm, non-tender mass felt 4 cm below the right costal margin; no jaundice, fever, or itching. Ultrasound today: a 6.8 cm solid, heterogeneous mass in liver segments IV and V that cannot be separated from the gallbladder, which contains stones; the rest of the liver is smooth, with no ascites. Multiphase CT, tumor markers, hepatitis serology and medical oncology consultation arranged

assessment_plan.display: Adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder invading the liver
assessment_plan.assessment: CT and MRI show a 7.1 cm mass arising from the gallbladder fundus and invading liver segments IVb and V, with gallstones and two enlarged hepatoduodenal ligament nodes (1.6 and 1.3 cm); the bile ducts are not dilated, the main portal vein and hepatic artery are free, and there are no other liver lesions. The liver is smooth, without cirrhosis. CT of the chest shows only a 6 mm calcified granuloma in the right upper lobe. The core biopsy shows moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, CK7 positive, CK20 and CDX2 negative, consistent with a pancreatobiliary origin; with the imaging, this is a primary gallbladder adenocarcinoma, not a primary liver cancer. Alpha-fetoprotein is normal and CA 19-9 412 U/mL. Clinical T3 N1 M0 (stage IIIB) on imaging. Liver function is preserved: Child-Pugh A6 (albumin 3.4 g/dL), ALBI grade 2, bilirubin and INR normal. Dr. Choi recommends tumor board review and a staging laparoscopy before any attempt at resection, because peritoneal disease is often not seen on CT in this cancer, and genomic profiling of the biopsy tissue. He agreed

He is not short of breath, even on the stairs, and has no chest pain, diarrhea, rash, or new abdominal pain. His appetite is a little lower but he is drinking well. Two colleagues at work have colds. He asked whether this could be pneumonitis from durvalumab and whether he needs antibiotics.

referral.question: A solid 6.8 cm mass in liver segments IV and V, inseparable from a gallbladder containing stones, in a 57-year-old man with three months of right upper abdominal aching, early fullness and 4 kg weight loss. He trained and briefly practiced as a physician. Multiphase CT, tumor markers and hepatitis serology are under way. Please establish the diagnosis, stage the disease, take him to the tumor board, and advise on treatment
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, with the CT and any biopsy result
referral.pertinent_history: Dull ache under the right ribs and early fullness for about three months; 4 kg weight loss; no jaundice, fever, itching or vomiting. Examination: a firm, non-tender mass 4 cm below the right costal margin; no ascites or nodes. Ultrasound today: a 6.8 cm solid, heterogeneous mass in segments IV and V that cannot be separated from the gallbladder, which contains stones; the rest of the liver smooth. Results today: hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, platelets 342 x10^3/uL, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL, albumin 3.4 g/dL, bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 212 U/L, AST 48 U/L, ALT 41 U/L, INR 1.0, alpha-fetoprotein 3.2 ng/mL, CA 19-9 412 U/mL, CEA 8.6 ng/mL. Hepatitis B and C serology sent. Never smoked; alcohol rarely. Acetaminophen as needed. No known allergies. ECOG 1. He leads a political organization and works full days. As a physician by training he asks to see his images and results, wants plain information, and wants to be cared for on the standard pathway

consultant_note.history: Mr. Sun, a 57-year-old political leader who trained and briefly practiced in medicine, is seen at the request of Dr. Huang two weeks after presenting with three months of right upper abdominal aching, early fullness and 4 kg weight loss and a palpable mass. He has had a multiphase CT, MRI with MRCP and an ultrasound-guided core biopsy. He has no jaundice, itching, fever or vomiting, and works full days. He reviewed the images with us and asked for a plain account
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Multiphase CT of the liver with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis: a 7.1 cm mass arising from the gallbladder fundus and invading liver segments IVb and V, gallstones, two enlarged hepatoduodenal ligament nodes (1.6 and 1.3 cm), main portal vein and hepatic artery free, no other liver lesions, no ascites, a 6 mm calcified granuloma in the right upper lobe. MRI with MRCP: the mass arises from the gallbladder wall; no bile duct dilation; liver smooth without cirrhosis. Core biopsy: moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, CK7 positive, CK20 and CDX2 negative. Alpha-fetoprotein 3.2 ng/mL, CA 19-9 412 U/mL, CEA 8.6 ng/mL. Albumin 3.4 g/dL, bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, INR 1.0, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, core antibody positive, surface antibody 85 mIU/mL, HBV DNA undetectable; hepatitis C antibody negative

assessment.display: Adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder invading the liver
assessment.assessment: This is not a primary liver cancer. In a liver without cirrhosis the imaging criteria for hepatocellular carcinoma do not apply and tissue is needed; the biopsy shows an adenocarcinoma with a pancreatobiliary pattern, the imaging shows it arising from the gallbladder wall, and alpha-fetoprotein is normal. This is a primary gallbladder adenocarcinoma invading the liver, clinical T3 N1 M0 (stage IIIB) on imaging. Gallbladder cancer often has peritoneal spread that CT does not show, so a staging laparoscopy should come before any attempt at resection. If there is no metastatic disease, an extended cholecystectomy with resection of segments IVb and V and portal lymphadenectomy could be curative in intent; if there is, treatment is systemic: gemcitabine and cisplatin with durvalumab is the preferred first-line regimen. Genomic profiling of the biopsy now will save time if a targeted treatment becomes relevant

Resolved past infection with undetectable HBV DNA and preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A6, ALBI grade 2). It does not limit surgery or chemotherapy. The reactivation risk with gemcitabine, cisplatin and durvalumab is low to moderate; monitoring HBV DNA and ALT every 3 months, with entecavir if HBV DNA becomes detectable, is appropriate. Hepatitis C is excluded

recommendations: Multidisciplinary hepatobiliary tumor board review this week
Staging laparoscopy before any resection, with biopsy of any peritoneal disease and an implanted port placed under the same anesthetic

If there are no metastases: extended cholecystectomy with resection of liver segments IVb and V and portal lymphadenectomy, then adjuvant treatment; if there are metastases: gemcitabine 1,000 mg/m2 and cisplatin 25 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 with durvalumab 1,500 mg on day 1 every 21 days for up to 8 cycles, then durvalumab every 4 weeks
Comprehensive genomic profiling of the biopsy tissue now (HER2, mismatch repair and microsatellite status, FGFR2, IDH1, BRAF, NTRK, RET, KRAS, tumor mutational burden)
HBV DNA and ALT every 3 months during treatment and for 6 to 12 months after, with entecavir if HBV DNA becomes detectable or surface antigen reappears
Specialist palliative care alongside treatment as soon as advanced disease is confirmed, or earlier if he wishes
Results shared with him in full and in person, with his images, by one coordinating clinician; the same pathway and the same thresholds as for any patient
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Huang, who sees him the same day. Mr. Sun reviewed the images and the pathology with us. We explained why a staging laparoscopy comes before any operation, what each result would mean for treatment, and that the aim of treatment would be decided by that result. He asked to hear results himself first and to decide who else is told; he agreed to the plan. He decides who receives this note
consultant_note.follow_up: Tumor board this week; staging laparoscopy in about ten days; review with Dr. Huang and the oncology team in two weeks with the result to decide treatment
